analysis.one_liner: Raises the required fuel economy for new passenger cars to 40 miles per gallon.
analysis.headline: The bill to require passenger cars to average 40 mpg by 2017 was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2007 and never received a vote or hearing before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Transportation Department to set a fuel economy standard of 40 miles per gallon for passenger cars made in model year 2017, up from the 27.5 mpg minimum then in effect. It also would have created a national registry for trading greenhouse gas credits, letting carmakers buy credits to cover up to 10% of their fuel economy requirement. The bill was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers would gain the most: a car meeting a 40 mpg standard uses roughly a third less fuel than one at the 27.5 mpg floor, cutting gas bills for years after purchase. Households and the country would also benefit from reduced oil consumption, including reduced reliance on petroleum produced outside the United States, and lower greenhouse gas emissions. A new industry of certified emissions registries and credit traders would also have gained business under the bill's registry system.

how_it_helps.text: Would have required the Transportation Secretary to set a passenger car fuel economy standard of 40 miles per gallon for model year 2017, up from the 27.5 mpg standard then in effect, cutting how much gasoline each new car burns.

Would have pushed automakers to reduce oil use, with the bill's stated purposes including reducing reliance by U.S. markets on petroleum produced outside the United States for vehicle fuel and cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

Included a cost safeguard for buyers: the Transportation Secretary could not issue a standard whose marginal costs exceed its marginal benefits, and would have had to give the Energy Department and EPA time to comment before finalizing any standard.

Would have created a national, voluntary registry for recording and trading verified greenhouse gas reductions, with an implementing panel in the Commerce Department setting conflict-of-interest and verification standards for certified registries.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of engineering cars to reach 40 mpg, and some of that cost would likely show up in higher new-car prices. Consumers buying new cars would pay those prices up front, though lower fuel use would offset them over the life of the vehicle. Taxpayers would fund the new registry, implementing panel, and rulemaking at the Transportation and Commerce Departments.

drawbacks.text: The 40 mpg mandate would impose real engineering costs on automakers, and some of that cost would likely be passed to buyers as higher prices for new cars, which falls hardest on people who need to replace an old vehicle sooner rather than later.

The bill would have let manufacturers purchase greenhouse gas credits through the new registry to satisfy up to 10% of their fuel economy requirement, meaning some cars would get no more efficient at all and the money would flow to credit traders instead of engineering.

The voluntary registry would credit emission reductions against any future mandatory greenhouse gas program, which invites companies to record cuts they would have made anyway and redeem them later, weakening whatever mandate eventually arrives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is honest and favorable: higher fuel economy standards cost automakers and raise new-car prices somewhat, but save drivers money at the pump every year and cut oil use. The bill's weak points are the credit-purchase loophole (capped at 10% of the standard) and a voluntary registry that banks reductions against future mandates, both of which give industry room to pay rather than improve. On balance the fuel savings would likely outweigh the price effects for most buyers, but the design leaves the door open to paper compliance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the full two-year Congress without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Stevens of Alaska introduced the bill on January 4, 2007, the first day of the 110th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The bill would have required a 40 mpg passenger car standard for model year 2017 and created a national greenhouse gas credit registry, with automakers allowed to apply purchased credits toward up to 10% of their fuel economy obligation.
Only one Republican Senator cosponsored the bill.
The Commerce Committee took no further action on the bill, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died: they never faced a 40 mpg mandate or the compliance costs that would have come with it. Drivers lost the fuel savings and emissions reductions the standard would have delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, who avoided the 40 mpg mandate

for.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke on introduction; it was his only action of substance on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Daniel Inouye, D-HI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Fought higher fuel economy mandates during this period; no action by them on this specific bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill was sponsored by a Republican with a single Republican cosponsor and stalled in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have required passenger cars to average 40 mpg by model year 2017, forcing investment in more efficient vehicles; the credit-trading provision would have let carmakers buy their way out of up to 10% of that obligation.

industries.industry: Emissions registries and greenhouse gas credit traders
industries.note: The bill creates a national registry, a certification process for registries, and rules letting manufacturers trade and buy greenhouse gas credits, building the infrastructure of a new emissions-trading market.

Cars averaging 40 mpg burn substantially less gasoline than cars at the 27.5 mpg floor, shrinking demand for the industry's core product; the bill explicitly aims to reduce reliance on petroleum for vehicle fuel.
